A zone can be drawn with or without a **border**, and both are good choices. A
highlight behind a line reads better with no border. If you want its edges
drawn, two `rule`s do it better than a border: they can be dashed, and each is
at a real value on the axis. The target band comes from the `target_band` table,
shown in [A band across the panel](#a-band-across-the-panel). The rules read a
table of two rows, one for each edge, written inside the sentence:

```{r}
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(lower, upper) + style(color = "seagreen") +
  data(data.frame(sales = c(150, 175)), name = "edges") + rule +
    style(color = "seagreen", pattern = "dashed") +
  line + point +
  y_label("Sales") + title("A zone for the region, rules for its edges")
```

*"Given quarterly: x is year, y is sales, a target zone from lower to upper; then
given two rows with sales 150 and 175: rules colored seagreen, with pattern
dashed; then given quarterly again: a line and points."*

The two marks read their positions differently, which is why the edges need a
table of their own. A zone is told which columns hold its sides, with
`bounds(lower, upper)`. A rule takes its direction from its table instead
([Horizontal or vertical](rule.qmd#horizontal-or-vertical)). The plot's `y` is
`sales`, and the `edges` table has a `sales` column and no `year` column. So
each rule marks a value of `sales` and spans the panel. The rule
chapter draws the same two marks over a scatter of life expectancy, in
[Thickness as data](rule.qmd#thickness-as-data).

But the mark is not only a highlight. It draws the candlestick, the heatmap's
cells, [the icicle](../transforms.qmd#partition-a-whole-among-nested-parts) and
the [mosaic](../transforms.qmd#the-mosaic), and in every one of those the zone
*is* the data rather than a background behind it. There the composition above
cannot help. A rule spans the whole panel, or makes a short tick at its edge, so
it cannot outline one cell of a mosaic. So a zone takes `style(border_color = ,
border_size = )`, like `bar`, `box`, `point` and `surface`. The plot outlines the
two slumps of the `recessions` table, shown in
[A band up the panel](#a-band-up-the-panel):

```{r}
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(recessions) + zone * bounds(start = start, end = end) +
    style(border_color = "black") +
  line +
  y_label("Sales") + title("A zone with a border of its own")
```

*"Given quarterly: x is year, y is sales, recession zones from start to end,
with border color black, and also a line."*

Both choices stay available, and which one is right depends on whether the zone
is the background or the subject. By default a zone has no border: with no
`border_color` and no `border_size`, it draws no outline.

The [grid of every mark and every setting](../style.qmd#what-you-can-set) shows
which other marks share this list. What a mark *maps* rather than sets is its
row on the [grid of marks and channels](../combinations.qmd#marks-and-channels).

## What it refuses {#what-it-refuses}

A `point` or a `line` needs only the plot's `x` and `y`, so the first thing to
try is a `zone` with no transform on the same table. It is refused. A continuous
value marks a single point, so two continuous positions give a rectangle no
width and no height:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) + zone + line
```

A categorical column on one axis and a continuous one on the other do not make a
cell either. The category gives the zone its sides on its own axis, but a
continuous column gives it none on the other. Here that column is `year`, and
gog refuses the sentence rather than drop a column you wrote. The message names
three ways to fix it. First, cut `year` into ranges with `zone * bin * mean`, as
in the [summary heatmap](#cells-cut-then-summarized-the-summary-heatmap).
Second,
[store `year` as a categorical column](../data.qmd#declaring-the-order-of-categories) before plotting. If a cell then holds more than one row, write `zone * mean`. Without it, gog refuses the sentence rather than show only the last row in each cell. Third, leave out `x(year)` and `color(life)`, so that the zone has only `y(continent)`. Each zone then fills its slot across the whole panel, as in the [column highlight](#one-slot-a-column-highlight):

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gm_all) + zone + x(year) + y(continent) + color(life)
```

`bounds()` takes its columns in pairs, so one column is not enough. The refusal
names the half you gave, here `lower`, and lists the pairs that complete it:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(lower = lower) +
  line
```

A `zone` with `bounds()` reads a position in only two cases: when a categorical
column or a column of dates gives it slots, and when the position names one of
its own sides, such as `y(lower)`. gog refuses a position that no layer reads.
So the `score_band` table from [A band up the panel](#a-band-up-the-panel),
written as a zone with `x(score)`, is refused. The zone takes its sides from
`lower` and `upper`, and `score` places nothing:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(score_band) + zone * bounds(lower, upper) + x(score)
```

The `start`/`end` pair bounds the axis that does not carry the measure. In the
[candlestick](#the-candlestick) that is `x`, which holds the 14 sessions as
categories. Write `open` and `close` in that pair, and gog reads each price as a
place among the sessions. There are only 14 sessions, so a price near 100 points
far beyond the last one, off the panel, and gog refuses the sentence:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(candles) + zone * bounds(start = open, end = close) + x(session)
```

The message suggests the other pair, `bounds(open, close)`, which bounds the
measure axis, as the candlestick does.

A zone needs two things from its transforms: where its cells are, and what each
cell shows. `bounds` gives only where. `count` and `proportion` give only what,
inside the cells your categories already make. `density` gives both. `bin` gives
both, or only where when `mean` follows it, as in `bin * mean`. Two transforms
that give the same thing contradict each other, and gog refuses the pair. `mean`
gives only what, yet `bounds * mean` is refused too. `bounds` makes one
rectangle per row, and `mean` makes one per cell your positions make, so the
sentence says what the rectangle is twice:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(lower, upper) * mean +
  line
```

To shade a region the data *computed* rather than one you chose, use
[`ribbon`](ribbon.qmd). For example, `ribbon * range` fills between the minimum
and the maximum at each `x`. A zone with `bounds` shades where you say, and a
ribbon shades between values a transform computed from the rows.

Asking for two measurements is also a contradiction. `count` writes one
measurement and `mean` writes another, but a cell holds a single number. `count`
makes no cells of its own, so once `mean` measures the cells, `count` has
nothing left to do:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(winds) + zone * count * mean + x(direction) + y(season) + color(speed)
```

`bin * mean`, in [the summary
heatmap](#cells-cut-then-summarized-the-summary-heatmap), has the same shape as
`count * mean` but is not a contradiction: `bin` makes the cells, and `mean`
measures inside them.

Write `mean` with no column to reduce, and gog asks for the column rather than
guessing. A zone measures by `color`, so the refusal asks you to name the column
in `color()`:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(winds) + zone * mean + x(direction) + y(season)
```

`bounds` names the sides from columns you hold, and `bin` cuts sides from the
data, so `bounds * bin` says where the sides are twice. gog does not pick one of
the two, and refuses the sentence:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(quarterly) + x(year) + y(sales) +
  data(target_band) + zone * bounds(lower, upper) * bin +
  line
```

A `bin` needs something to cut, and two categorical axes leave it nothing. Each
category is one slot, and a slot cannot be cut smaller. A cell for each pair of
categories is the tile plot, which needs no binning. So the refusal names
`count`, which tallies the rows into the cells the categories already make:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(six_weeks) + zone * bin + x(weekday) + y(week)
```

`zone * bin` does draw with one categorical axis and one continuous axis: that
is [the mixed mesh](#one-of-each-the-mixed-mesh). `zone * density` does not. A
density is estimated *between* the data points, so each axis must give it an
interval to spread along, and a category gives none. A density for each category
is a different plot, so the refusal names what to use instead:
`line * density + color(continent)`, a density curve for each category:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gm_all) + zone * density + x(life) + y(continent)
```

`bin(tiling = "hex")` is refused on the mixed mesh. A hexagonal mesh shifts
every second row by half a cell, and its rows fit into each other. So each
hexagon reaches partly into the space between its neighbors. On a categorical
axis there is no such space: nothing lies between Asia and Europe. A category's
slots have an order but no distance, so the mixed mesh always has rectangular
cells:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(tiling = "hex") + x(life) + y(continent)
```

`count` over two continuous axes is the opposite of `bin` over two categorical
axes. `count` tallies rows into cells that already exist, and a continuous value
marks a point, which owns no cell. So the refusal names `bin`, which cuts the
cells first:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gm_all) + zone * count + x(gdp) + y(life)
```

The six summaries, such as `mean`, follow the same rule. `mean` reduces a column
inside a cell, and a continuous position gives it no cell. The refusal names two
fixes: a category on each position, or `bin` on the continuous axis first:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(winds) + zone * mean + x(bearing) + y(season) + color(speed)
```

`zone * bin` already measures each cell by its count, and the count goes to
`color`. Binning replaces each cell's rows with one count, so `color(continent)`
has no rows left to read:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gm_all) + zone * bin + x(gdp) + y(life) + color(continent)
```

A tiling that gog does not offer is refused, and the message lists the two that
it does offer, `rect` and `hex`. gog does not quietly draw rectangles instead:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(gm_all) + zone * bin(tiling = "octagon") + x(gdp) + y(life)
```

On a zone, `density(bandwidth = )` is refused for a reason of its own. A
bandwidth is a width in one column's units, and a zone's density spreads over
two columns, which measure different things. One number cannot be a width in
both, so gog refuses it:

```{r}
#| error: true
data(iris_flowers) + zone * density(bandwidth = 0.5) +
  x(sepal_length) + y(petal_length)
```

That is why [the density section](#cells-the-data-estimated-zone-density) uses
`adjust`: it multiplies the width that gog picks for each axis, so it means the
same on both.

## In short {#in-short}

A zone's sides come from five places: `bounds`, `bin`, `density`, a category's
slot, or a boundary named by `group`. `partition` and `flow` compute whole
rectangles themselves. Where nothing gives sides, the zone
reaches the panel edge, which a `ribbon` cannot do. The pair you name decides
which axis it bounds; the column types decide which one measures.

## What comes next {#what-comes-next}

A zone shows a measure as a color, and you read its value from the legend.
[Surface](surface.qmd) gives that measure a height instead, and the same field
is raised into the cube as a sheet.
